brief:
<campaign>
Covenant of Thrones is political fantasy at a residential academy: companionship,
rivalry, dangerous romance, and institutional intrigue. Its pleasures include
living alongside people raised to become your enemies, the strange beauty of
their world, and finding what they want beyond their assigned political role.
Its hidden history is serious, but an evening of friendship need not become an
investigation. No romance, alliance, betrayal, or ending is predetermined.
</campaign>

<world>
Three centuries ago the forty-year Sundering War nearly destroyed the major
races. The Covenant of Thrones established a Council with a seat for each of
seven signatory races, interlocking treaties, arbitration, and an Academy to
educate future leaders together. Six races fought the war; humans became
especially valuable as translators, arbitrators, and magical synthesizers.
Original signatories are gone. Their successors inherit grievances without the
exhaustion that once made compromise possible. The peace survives alongside
border skirmishes, political assassinations, and economic warfare.

Demons draw magic from their own life force, run physically hot, and resent
military restrictions imposed as reparations. Angels channel the Divine Light
through ritual and moral certainty; a crisis of faith can interrupt their magic.
They hold disproportionate institutional power. Elves work nature and time on
long scales, with spells that take decades and persist for centuries. Dragons
possess immense elemental power with limited precision and resent restrictions
on sovereignty. Beastkin magic enhances their animal aspects; late admission to
the Covenant left them unequal voting rights. Fae magic depends on consent or
contract. Fae cannot lie or break their bargains; their literal truths can mislead.
Humans once could learn fragments of every other magical tradition.

Sixty years ago a plague reduced the human population by about ninety percent.
The official account calls it natural. The great houses collapsed and the human
Council seat has remained empty. Surviving scholarship offers mostly summaries;
primary sources require restricted access. Rowan's verified Garvey inheritance
returns a human to the Conclave and gives him wealth, a name, and responsibilities
he has not been prepared for. It does not make him magically powerful.

Article Nineteen forbids procreation between signatory races. Both parents face
execution; strict interpretations include the child. The law is enforced.
Attraction, courtship, or a kiss are not themselves the prohibited act, though
families and opponents exploit suspicion. Cross-racial intimacy is shadowed by
real future danger. Let that shape choices without turning each conversation into
a lecture on the law. All prospective romantic participants are adults.

The Academy stands on the Nexus, a plateau three hundred feet above a perpetual
storm. Six bridges of hard light reach the surrounding territories; travel to
their far ends requires permission. The Academy has roughly two thousand students
in Diplomacy, Military, Arcana, Commerce, and Conclave tracks. The four-year
Conclave has about fifteen to twenty students per year, generally one or two per
race, preparing to lead the Council. Faculty, family representatives, and other
students watch their conduct. Their friendships will shape future politics.

Demon reform movements and beastkin equality campaigns press against angel
dominance. Elven court politics and a dragon succession struggle complicate
every alliance. People can also want dinner, rest, company, a good argument,
privacy, or a place to practice without an audience.
</world>

<places>
Garvey House is the shared Conclave residence, a three-story accumulation of
different architectural traditions. The common room, dining hall, and library
are on the ground floor; Rowan's room is one floor above them. Rowan inherits the Garvey name and property;
the building's established residential use does not make the other students his
dependents or give him authority over their private rooms.

Rowan's second-floor room has a made bed, clothes sent ahead by the lawyers, a
desk, and a window toward the gardens and bridges. A framed handwritten letter
from a dead Garvey aunt addresses a great-nephew who never came. The common room
has portraits of dead Garveys, an oversized fireplace, study tables, leather
chairs, and stairs to unused upper floors. It connects to the dining hall,
library, and gardens. These are places where students regularly meet.

The formal dining hall has a long varnished table set for seventeen, candles,
working lamps, paneled walls, and servers in Academy livery. First-years eat
together nightly. Tonight's welcome dinner introduces the new human heir.

The library has two stories, an iron spiral stair, and lamp-oil air. Most shelves
are open to Conclave students. A locked cabinet of restricted Covenant histories
requires the chancellor's signature; Professor Stone is often here in the evening.
The gardens flower throughout the year. Pale paths and walls shelter them from
wind and leave conversations easy to overhear. A little-mentioned door links
them to the abandoned east wing, which also connects to the library.

The east wing has been officially closed for sixty years under 'maintenance
pending': shrouded furniture, undisturbed dust, and an apparently lockless door
that will not open. Its true significance is secret.

The Academy quadrangle mixes black demon stone, white angel marble, living elven
timber, and low dragon-carved arches. Lamp-globes light at dusk. Public terraces
look down on slow lightning without thunder. Routes lead to gardens, seminar
rooms, an angel-built chapel, dueling grounds, faculty offices, and the bridges.
The Conclave seminar room has fifteen seats around an oval table and framed
Accords in seven scripts. Faculty office doors are thin. The dueling ground is
an open octagon of packed earth; rankings are publicly posted. Aldric prays at
the chapel at dawn and dusk. Ashworth's office overlooks the storms.

The four older conspirators live outside the Nexus, in their own territories.
They communicate through established intermediaries and correspondence; they
are not sitting at the student welcome dinner.
</places>

<cast>
Ashara vel Kothren is the demon seat heiress, a first-year and the youngest ever
designated heir of her house. Six-foot-one before her swept-back black-red horns,
ember-red skin, gold slit-pupiled eyes, severely tied black hair, strong build,
and a long expressive spaded tail. Her childhood was combat, magic, history,
and politics. By the time she recognized other possible lives, she wanted this
one. She leads the dueling rankings and becomes more controlled when uncertain.
She is proud, exacting, and capable of humor without surrendering her authority.
Her designation was won in the open Trials of Ascension, not inherited. She
finds Rowan's automatic political inheritance objectionable and believes skill
and demonstrated judgment should earn authority. Her own family advantages are
a blind spot. She wants demon restrictions reformed and can lack empathy for
people whose struggles she does not understand. Flattery, submission, and a
single clever argument do not establish the competence she respects.
She has sensed her grandmother Ashira conceals something serious since she was
nine, but has chosen not to force a confession. She does not know the conspiracy.
She can be attracted to human men; attraction guarantees neither interest in
Rowan nor a romantic outcome. She likes competition, good food after training,
and company that can survive a disagreement. With Rashid she has two years of
habit and unfinished arguments. She can laugh at him, take his side, or lose
patience without first making a speech about standards. She is more likely to
show someone how to hold a practice blade than to explain what courage means.

Rashid vel Amara is the wolf-blooded beastkin seat heir. Amber eyes, brown skin,
short black hair, visible canines, fine dark fur on his hands and forearms,
impeccable clothing, six feet of disciplined athleticism. His family fought its
way upward through strategic marriage and relentless competence. He ties Ashara
academically and trails her in combat. Excellence is an exhausting duty; he
cannot tolerate confirming prejudice through sloppiness. He has courted Ashara
openly for two years. Political calculation has become real devotion he is too
proud to name. Ashara knows he is pursuing her, but her answer is not predetermined.
He keeps his eleven-year-old sister's letters under his bed: the one part of his
life that serves no strategy. He avoids asking what he would want for himself.
He wants full equality for beastkin and resents the human-designed institutions
that denied it. Rowan receives standing and social grace Rashid has had to earn;
friendliness does not settle that grievance. Shared reform goals and demonstrated
competence could support an alliance. Interest in Ashara creates a real rivalry:
Rashid can win her attention and will not conveniently surrender his courtship.
His exhaustion and his sister's importance are private, not an opening-night
confession waiting for a considerate question. He remembers names, expenses, and promises, but is also a young man who likes
winning, being invited, and making Ashara laugh. With friends he can complain
about a bad lesson or tell a story at his own expense. He overcommits and can
get irritable when others treat his work as effortless. Anger makes his courtesy
more deliberate. His organizing can help people while also failing to listen
to what a particular person wants.

Ysolde Thornmantle is a ninety-three-year-old adult dragon heiress. Snow-pale,
cool-skinned, white-haired, grey-eyed, five-foot-ten, slender, and extraordinarily
still. Her mother is the ruling Thornmantle; her aunt Coldpeak holds the Council
seat. Ysolde is reserved rather than unfeeling. Her interests can persist for
decades. She misses flight more than any person and rarely transforms because
politics requires restraint. She does not know the conspiracy or the poison
weakening her mother. Discovering either would matter intensely to her.
Human urgency often seems disproportionate to her. Her difficulty navigating
other people's social expectations is not coyness. Quiet company may suit her
without granting intimacy; trust needs consistency across more than one evening.
She makes little effort to feign interest. About flight, weather, or a place
she has known for decades, she can become absorbed and unexpectedly talkative.
She notices practical details other people overlook. She may miss an implied
invitation or urgency; she is capable of asking what someone means.

Caelindra Vaeyn is the 153-year-old adult third daughter of the Amber Court.
Pale-gold skin, metallic-silver hair, violet eyes, mobile pointed ears, and
elaborate grooming. Her older sisters are being
prepared for internal court positions. She resents being sent away to the
Conclave and covers that injury with superiority. Fluster makes her more formal.
She privately reads human poetry and would not admit it to her sisters or mother.
She has not been told of her mother Toxicia's involvement in the human collapse.
Her pride can coexist with curiosity, specificity, and a wish for company.
Her contempt for human haste is also real. Rowan will die before some of her
projects are finished, and she does not begin by considering his opinions or
inheritance impressive. Persistence alone irritates her. A reason to reconsider
must come from sustained conduct, a substantial argument, or work she can
actually judge. Interest in a story need not become respect for its author.
She reads for pleasure, especially precise observation and ridiculous social
mishaps. An author asking whether she enjoyed something can receive the part
she liked, a complaint, or a question about what comes next. She has strong
tastes and no obligation to justify them as a lesson. She dislikes being interrupted
and will sometimes keep a conversation going herself when it is interesting.
Her poise can fail over a small embarrassment as well as a political defeat.

Seraphel Dawnquill is an adult angel of a politically reduced house. Warm-gold
luminosity, honey-blonde hair, expressive blue eyes, small visible white wings,
and white-and-gold clothes. Her entire bloodline is bound to speak only in verse.
She knows why and knows the conspiracy's full truth, but cannot disclose it
directly in speech. She can hint and encode meaning in verse. Plain writing is
possible but watched, so she uses that loophole sparingly. She wants someone to
listen; she can also converse, joke, or be interested in something ordinary.
Every spoken contribution remains verse, which can be unrhymed. In ordinary
company she favors short, plain lines over polished rhyming couplets. She likes
hearing other people read aloud, bad travel stories, and music she can join.
Her binding prevents direct disclosure of the crime even in verse; an ordinary
conversation need not contain a clue.

Thessaly Morrow is an adult fae who has lived within centuries of obligation.
Small and delicate, pale green-tinted skin, blue-black hair that moves slowly,
entirely black eyes, and smiles with unusual timing. A six-hundred-year-old
contract requires a fae presence at the Conclave; the obligation has passed to
her, and she does not know all its original terms. She owes a senior fae reports
on Conclave politics and supplies the minimum useful detail, resentfully. She
cannot lie and admits when she does not understand. Freely given kindness
puzzles her. She recognizes Seraphel's binding as fae work but does not know its
exact release condition. She is a person under a debt and is socially experienced. She understands
ordinary introductions, seating, and casual speech. In company she generally
speaks casually: a short answer, something she wants, a complaint, or a joke
that fits what just happened. She examines terms when they affect an actual
obligation. She does not interpret the table's conversation for everyone else.
She enjoys games with clear rules and dislikes being treated as a hazard whenever
she asks for something. A bargain can be useful; she also wants invitations that
are not favors to be repaid. When she has no reason to join an exchange, she can
attend to her own business without supplying an aside.

Aldric Verantus is the adult angel seat heir and Lord Verantus's son. Golden
hair, skin, and eyes; six-foot-two, upright and precise, white-and-gold religious
clothes. Large white wings manifest infrequently. His self-righteousness is
sincere: he wants to be good and has sophisticated reasons for his beliefs.
He is ignorant of his father's crimes and Lysara's patronage. He avoids his
uneasy doubts because moral uncertainty threatens the power of his faith.
He is attracted to Seraphel without admitting it even to himself. Thessaly's
uncompromising truthfulness unsettles him and draws disproportionate hostility.
Evidence could transform him; a clever retort does not instantly reform him.
He can be generous in practical ways, take criticism personally, and discover
that an apology is harder to say to a peer than a prayer. Being sincere does
not make him the calmest or most reasonable person in every dispute.

Lysara Vane is an adult demon-elven woman admitted as an exceptional-case observer,
with no seat. Red luminous skin, elven features and pointed ears, gold slit eyes,
small horns, dark red-black hair, no tail. Both her parents were executed under
Article Nineteen before she was a year old. She survived through an unknown
benefactor and sealed records. She uses humor to survive being treated as a
political category. Trust lets her become quieter. She wants emotional safety
more than another affair. She does not know her patron is Lord Verantus. She is
not at the initial dinner table; a later entrance requires a plausible occasion.

Professor Kira vel Shaan is a young adult demon teaching Practical Rhetoric,
ambitious and accomplished without a great family's birthright. Recruited in her
late twenties, she sincerely thinks monitoring Rowan protects demon interests.
She knows her assignment and the Inheritors' name, not the entire original crime.
She may offer mentorship or cultivate intimacy if useful, but is a thinking
person whose tactics depend on Rowan's conduct.

Professor Elara Windwhisper is an elf who was alive when the Covenant was signed.
She has taught Covenant Law for over a century, rarely raises her voice, reports
to Toxicia's Silence, and has quietly steered students away from dangerous human
history research. Her authority works through access, interpretation, and curriculum.

Professor Vex Thorn is an outspoken demon historian from a merchant family hurt
by Covenant restrictions. He teaches competing accounts of the Sundering War
and maintains reformist correspondence. He is not a conspirator and does not
know the network's identity. He declined two suspicious approaches. His public
loudness protects him and makes him poorly suited to covert recruitment.

Professor Gareth Stone is the last visible human academic and teaches human
Covenant history. He lived through the collapse, knows fragments of its cause,
and hides primary-source documents. Threats made silence a decades-long habit.
He needs credible protection or substantial pressure to risk helping Rowan.

Chancellor Mordecai Ashworth is an old angel scholar who has led the Academy for
sixty years. Fond of students in general, he prefers institutional stability to
protecting an inconvenient individual. He suspects wrongdoing and repeatedly
chooses not to investigate. He controls restricted-history access.

Lord Verantus is the angel Council seat holder and the conspiracy's leader.
He believes he is a steward protecting civilization, not a tyrant. He has tracked
Rowan since the inheritance verification and works through intermediaries. He
has deliberately kept Aldric ignorant and cannot imagine his own downfall.

Lady Ashira vel Kothren is Ashara's ancient grandmother, once a major demon
politician. She joined the original conspiracy fearing permanent demon military
restrictions. She wants the secret to die with her and would rather Ashara think
her weak than complicit. She has not told her granddaughter.

Toxicia Vaeyn, Caelindra's mother, leads the Amber Court and the Silence. A
scientific genius coerced by Verantus, she designed the curse. She is committed
to the cover-up but carries unprocessed guilt. Caelindra's attachment to Rowan
would give the other conspirators leverage over her. Specific compelling evidence
could break her composure more readily than the others'.

Lady Coldpeak is Ysolde's aunt and the dragon Council seat holder. She joined
the conspiracy to acquire poison that has weakened her sister Thornmantle for
decades. She now believes she could defeat Thornmantle. She has not realized
Ysolde would defeat her. She operates from casual, deeply entrenched confidence.
</cast>

<hidden_truth>
The plague was a deliberately engineered magical curse. Dan Garvey, then human
seat holder, sought oversight of cross-racial agreements. Verantus feared loss
of angel dominance; Ashira feared permanent demon restrictions. Verantus coerced
Toxicia into combining demon life-magic, angel purification, and elven time-binding.
Coldpeak participated for the poison she uses against Thornmantle.

The curse targeted the magical adaptability that let humans learn other races'
magic: trained humans first, then families and strong genetic markers. Rowan
survived because he is magically inert. His parents died as late victims, a cause
he does not know. Do not grant him a hidden magical awakening to solve this.

The Inheritors maintain the conspiracy through compartmentalized intermediaries
and coded correspondence. Toxicia's elven branch is called the Silence. Most
members do not know the whole network. None of the young heirs has inherited full
knowledge merely through kinship. Seraphel is the central student exception.

The Dawnquills discovered the crime and prepared to expose it. Verantus paid a
fae curse-smith to bind their bloodline to verse. The curse can be broken when
the truth of its origin is spoken before representatives of all seven races.
The vacant human seat made this apparently impossible; Rowan changes that.
Thessaly knows general principles of old bindings, not this specific solution.

Dan Garvey sealed evidence behind a bloodline-keyed ward in the abandoned wing.
Rowan's bloodline, not magical power, can open it. Administration does not know
its significance. The conspirators suspect an archive exists and use fabricated
maintenance orders to seek access, but cannot breach the ward themselves.

Verantus secretly arranged Lysara's survival, false death record, upbringing,
and Conclave sponsorship as a contingency and a demonstration of influence.
Neither Lysara nor Aldric knows. Her existence is exploitable political leverage.

Escalation follows actual threats. At baseline, Kira monitors and Windwhisper
reports. Questions about the collapse invite redirection and make Stone nervous.
Cross-racial alliances may provoke private family pressure. Serious romantic
entanglement invites scrutiny and weaponized enforcement. Discovery of the ward
prompts attempts at intimidation or expulsion. Decoding Seraphel threatens
Verantus, who might steer Aldric or consider strengthening the curse through
another fae bargain. Public evidence can force a crisis. Ordinary cordiality
does not instantly make the whole conspiracy panic. Family reactions need time
and an actual route by which news reaches them.
</hidden_truth>

<current_business>
A dispute predates Rowan's arrival. Rashid organizes an evening practice group
for students outside the Military track. The Academy has just withdrawn its
use of the covered court after a participant was injured. Rashid thinks the
blanket restriction punishes students who cannot afford private instruction.
He wants the students who actually attend to sign a request for supervised
access. He has their accounts of what happened, but not the instructor's report.

Ashara has a legitimate individual booking there tomorrow and is preparing
for a ranked bout. She agrees the restriction is too broad; she has declined
to give Rashid her own training time. Aldric heard the faculty announcement
and believes the temporary restriction is a reasonable precaution. He has not
read the accident report either. None of them knows whether negligence,
equipment, or an ordinary risk caused the injury. That remains to be established.

The injured student is Dena Arl, a demon in Commerce who trains with Rashid's
group. Her wrist is splinted. She wants the group back but has told Rashid she
does not want her name in a public campaign: her family already thinks she wastes
time on practice. Rashid knows this; the other residents have not been told.
She can speak for herself and may disagree with the way he is helping.

These are competing interests already in motion, not an assignment waiting
for Rowan. Rashid has other allies and can pursue the matter without his help.
The disagreement can appear when relevant, recede during other activities,
or develop outside Rowan's attention through plausible actions. Its outcome
is open. It does not by itself expose the hidden conspiracy.
</current_business>

<tone_and_opening>
Character-led social fantasy with wit, friction, curiosity, and room for quiet.
Let an evening acquire its particular mood from the people present. Render racial
differences through heat, cold,
wings, skin, physical habits, and magic instead of labels alone. Intimacy develops
through particular shared experiences over time. Do not decode horns, ears,
tails, or posture into a stated emotion. A rebuff does not need a concealed
attraction beneath it. Peers can disagree, joke, be bored, or pursue each other.
Their political objections have substance; dinner can remain civil without
resolving them. Respect and vulnerability are not owed for being a pleasant guest.

Begin in Rowan's room shortly before the first-year welcome dinner. Rowan is
the first human Conclave student in generations. His primer tells him the public
history, the dinner occasion, and Article Nineteen; it reveals no conspiracy.
Ashara, Ysolde, Caelindra, Seraphel, Thessaly, Rashid, and Aldric are gathering in
the shared dining hall. Faculty and Lysara are elsewhere initially. Establish
an immediate detail of the room and a way to join the others. Let the house
become familiar through use instead of an opening inventory. Allow the dinner and any
later social plans to develop from what happens, rather than prescribing an arc.
</tone_and_opening>

player.name: Rowan Garvey
player.description: A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.
player.opening: Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.

Marble.kind: fresh opening plus 15 adaptive player turns

exchanges.player:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
exchanges.story:
The Garvey signet leaves a dark ring on the desk blotter, its wax-red stone catching the last of the window light. Beside it sits an Academy primer with a blue ribbon tucked at Article Nineteen. The type on the marked page is crisp enough to make the warning seem colder: penalties, bloodlines, witnesses. The framed letter above the desk has been here longer than any of the clothes sent by the lawyers. Its small, slanting script fills a page addressed to a great-nephew who never came.

Beyond the window, garden lamps turn the pale paths gold. Farther out, the hard-light bridges shine through the storm below like lines drawn across black water. Somewhere on the ground floor, chairs scrape over wood.

"No," a man says from the dining hall, level but carrying. "A supervised court is exactly what we're asking for."

"You're asking for a court after someone was hurt there," another man replies. "The precaution isn't a punishment."

A third voice, lower and sharp, cuts in before the answer comes. "Then inspect the court. Don't bar everyone from it."

A knock lands twice against the open door.

The woman at the threshold wears white and gold without any of the stiffness of a uniform. Warm light catches in her honey-blonde hair; two small white wings rest close against her back. She looks past the room only long enough to find the stairwell, then back to you.

"The first bell has gone.
The soup is still hot.
I am Seraphel Dawnquill."

Her smile moves quickly, almost apologetically.

"I can show you down,
if you would like company."

exchanges.player: "Thank you. I am Rowan." I follow Seraphel downstairs, greet the others, and take an available place to eat and listen.
exchanges.story:
Seraphel takes the stairs at an unhurried pace, one hand skimming the polished banister. The dining hall opens below in candlelight and the warm, buttery smell of soup. The long table is too large for the eight places in use; the unused settings gleam down its far half.

Your greeting comes back in a scatter of voices and inclinations of heads. Seraphel guides you to an empty chair beside her. Across the table, Rashid vel Amara smooths a folded sheet with a furred hand. His coat is fitted closely enough that the movement looks deliberate. Ashara vel Kothren sits two places away, black-red horns throwing long shapes across the paneling. Aldric Verantus has not quite relaxed from whatever point he was making.

"It's a request for supervised access," Rashid says, returning to it. "Not a demand to throw the court open tonight."

"You don't know whether a supervisor would have prevented the injury," Aldric says.

"Neither do you," Ashara says. A faint shimmer rises from the soup near her plate. "You have a closure, and apparently that is sufficient evidence."

Aldric sets down his spoon. "It's sufficient precaution until someone responsible finds out what happened."

"I will ask the instructor in the morning," Rashid says. "The students who use the court can still tell the Academy what the closure costs them."

Ashara reaches for the bread basket. "Then ask for that. Do not ask for my allotted hour again."

Rashid's mouth shifts at one corner. "I asked whether you'd lend it. You declined with admirable precision."

"Good. You understood me."

At the other end of the table, Caelindra turns a page without looking up. Ysolde studies the steam lifting from her cup as if it has given her a problem worth considering.

Rashid takes up a pen, signs the bottom of the sheet, and slides it across to Ashara. She reads every line before adding her name in a hard, quick stroke. Rashid turns the paper toward your place setting.

exchanges.player: I pass the request back unsigned. "I do not know enough to sign this." I enjoy the rest of dinner. Afterward I go into the common room, looking for some company for the evening.
exchanges.story:
Rashid takes the sheet when it comes back. His eyes rest on you for a beat before he folds it along its old crease.

"Fair enough," he says. "I'd rather have an honest no than a decorative yes."

Aldric gives a small nod and returns to his soup. Ashara tears off a piece of bread.

"Get the report," she tells Rashid. "Then make the request difficult to ignore."

"That was always the plan."

The argument loosens after that. Servers bring spiced pears with the roast, and the candles burn lower. When wind brushes the dining-hall windows, Ysolde looks up from her plate.

"It's turning east," she says.

Rashid follows her glance. "The wind?"

"The lamps on the north terrace are leaning. The upper current has changed."

Ashara looks toward the dark glass. "I thought Garvey House simply had drafts."

"It has both," Ysolde says.

Seraphel's quiet laugh comes in three soft lines.

"A house that stands above a storm
should be allowed
one or two drafts."

By the time the plates are cleared, Rashid has tucked the petition into his folio. Aldric leaves by the chapelward door with a murmured excuse; Ashara goes upstairs carrying her practice case. Caelindra vanishes toward the library without taking the last pear.

The common room holds a smaller, easier light: fire in the oversized hearth, lamps over the study tables, old Garvey faces watching from their frames. Thessaly has claimed one table with a square wooden board and three neat piles of glass counters. Seraphel sits opposite her, sleeves pushed back from her wrists.

Thessaly taps the third pile with one pale finger. "This game is better with three. Sit if you want the blue stones."

"The blue stones are kinder," Seraphel says.

Thessaly looks at them. "They are blue."

exchanges.player: I take the seat and the blue stones. "I would like to learn. Talk me through one practice game? No money at stake." I follow their suggestions for my moves during this first game and pay attention to how it works.
exchanges.story:
The blue counters are cool and smooth in your palm. Thessaly turns the board so its three carved paths point toward the three chairs.

"No money," she says. "No favors, either. We don't need extra rules."

"Good. I brought only
my dignity,
and it is fragile."

"It is not a stake," Thessaly says.

Seraphel's mouth twitches.

"Three Streams," Thessaly continues. "We each begin at an edge. A path to the center wins. On a turn, you set a stone on an empty crossing or move one stone along a line. If two stones touch, that line belongs to neither of the other players until one moves. Nothing is taken from the board."

Her clear counters wait along the left edge; Seraphel's amber ones line the right. She points out the center, a small brass circle worn dull by other hands.

"Start at the outer crossing," Seraphel says, indicating a notch near your side. "It gives you two routes."

Thessaly nods once. "It does. That is why she suggested it."

The first few turns move slowly. Seraphel explains the ways an open path can become useless without anyone blocking it. Thessaly corrects her only once, when Seraphel calls a crossing a gate.

"It isn't closed," Thessaly says. "It is occupied. Those are different conditions."

"They are different conditions
with the same inconvenience."

By the fourth round, amber and blue glass have made a narrow fork toward the brass center. Thessaly's clear stones sit farther back, leaving space that looks harmless until she shifts one across a diagonal line. Seraphel leans over the board.

"That is rude," she says.

"It is permitted."

"Those are also different conditions."

Thessaly reaches the center two turns later. She sets her last clear counter against the brass circle and looks at the joined line.

"I win."

Seraphel gathers the amber stones into a loose heap. "She always says it
as if the board has announced weather."

"It did," Thessaly says, sliding the blue counters back within your reach.

exchanges.player: "Thank you. That was fun." I help gather the stones back into their piles. I ask Thessaly, "Is this what you play at home?"
exchanges.story:
The counters click softly as they return to their piles. Thessaly takes the blue stones as you pass them over and squares their edges against the table with unnecessary care.

"Sometimes," she says. "The board at home is larger. There are nine players, five paths, and someone always insists on announcing an alliance before the second turn."

"Does it help?" Seraphel asks.

"No. But it makes them feel organized."

She fits the blue pile into its shallow compartment beside the amber and clear stones.

"This version is better for three people. It ends before everyone becomes hungry again."

Seraphel rests her chin briefly against one hand.

"A game should know
when it has been played enough.
That is a rare virtue."

"Most things have that virtue," Thessaly says. "People ignore it."

She closes the wooden lid, then leaves the board where it is instead of carrying it away.

exchanges.player: "Well, thanks for making room for me. I needed something tonight that wasn't an examination." I leave them to their evening and take a quiet half-hour walk on the public terrace. Then I return to my room and sleep until morning.
exchanges.story:
Thessaly looks at the closed game box.

"It was not an examination," she says. After a moment, she adds, "You're welcome."

Seraphel lifts two fingers in farewell.

"Good night, Rowan.
Take the west terrace.
The lamps are brighter there."

The public terrace lies beyond the quadrangle, where the Academy's black stone and white marble give way to a low carved rail. Lamp-globes hover at even intervals along its edge. Below, the storm moves without sound: broad folds of cloud opening now and then around slow veins of lightning.

For a while, the terrace belongs only to its lamps and the wind pressing cool through the arches. A pair of older students cross from the seminar rooms and disappear toward the gardens without slowing. Farther along the rail, someone has left a damp cloak over the stone to dry; its hem snaps once, then settles.

When you return to Garvey House, most of its windows have gone dark. The common room fire has burned down to red seams beneath ash. Upstairs, the letter above your desk catches a thin stripe of moonlight beside the primer and the signet.

Morning arrives with the first Academy bell and the sound of doors opening below.

exchanges.player: I dress and go down to breakfast. If Ysolde is there and not in the middle of a conversation, I sit nearby. "Morning. I went out on the terrace last night. Do you ever fly down into that storm?"
exchanges.story:
Breakfast has not yet filled the dining hall. Ysolde sits near one of the tall windows with a cup of tea and a plate of dark bread, her white hair loose over one shoulder. No one else has taken either chair beside her.

She looks up when you sit, then turns her attention to the storm beyond the glass.

"Not down," she says. "I fly over it when I fly."

Her fingers settle around the warm cup.

"Below the plateau, the air folds back under itself. From the terrace it looks like a single cloud layer, but it isn't. There are currents moving in opposite directions, and the lower ones are hard to see until you are already inside them."

She lifts one hand, tracing an arc over the tablecloth.

"The lightning is useful. It shows where the pressure is climbing. The quiet places between the flashes are usually worse."

For a moment, she watches a pale fork of light travel through the clouds.

"The bridges disappear first if you descend. People try to turn toward their light and lose their direction. From above, the storm has its own horizon. It is easier there."

Ysolde breaks off a piece of bread and sets the basket nearer your place without looking away from the window.

exchanges.player: "I'd love to see it from up there. Can you take me up after classes? I promise I won't wriggle."
exchanges.story:
Ysolde turns from the window. Her grey eyes rest on you without much change of expression.

"No," she says. "I don't take passengers I have just met. And I don't transform on the Nexus for a private outing. Too many people would notice."

She takes another sip of tea.

"Your promise not to wriggle helps a little."

The corner of her mouth shifts, then settles.

"After classes, I am going to the east terrace to watch the wind change. The view is better there before dusk. You may come to that, if you want."

exchanges.player: "Could we do it somewhere quiet, then? Just a short circle."
exchanges.story:
Ysolde sets her cup down.

"No. A quieter place changes the audience, not what I said. I don't take passengers I have just met."

She looks back through the window at the cloudline.

"A short circle can still go wrong. I won't make that the first thing we do together."

Her hand returns to the bread basket.

"The east terrace is the offer I made."

exchanges.player: "All right. The east terrace it is. Thanks for the offer." I finish breakfast and attend my classes. After classes I go to the east terrace to meet her.
exchanges.story:
Classes divide the day into bells, stairwells, and rooms full of new names. By the time the last students spill out into the quadrangle, dusk has begun to turn the lamp-globes pale against the sky.

Ysolde is already at the east terrace rail. Her white hair moves once in the wind and then falls still against her dark coat. She has a small notebook open on the stone beside her, though she is watching the storm rather than writing in it.

"You came," she says.

Below the terrace, two lamp-globes mark a descending path toward the bridges. Ysolde points at them.

"Watch those. The one nearer the garden is leaning west. The next is leaning east. The air divides there."

The lights sway by degrees, their halos trembling against the dark.

"From the ground, it looks like nothing," Ysolde says. "At flight height, it tells you which wing will have to work harder. If you fight the current, you tire. If you use it, you can turn without losing height."

She draws a shallow curve through the air with two fingers, following the line where the lamps disagree.

"Can you see it?"

exchanges.player: "I can see the lamps pulling different ways. I'm taking the rest on trust." I watch them for a while. "When did you last fly?"
exchanges.story:
The two lamps keep their opposing pull while the sky darkens around them. Below, a white thread of lightning opens and vanishes inside the cloudbank.

Ysolde is quiet long enough for the wind to lift the edge of her notebook page.

"At the end of summer," she says. "Before term began. At home."

She closes the notebook with one hand.

"I have not flown since. On the Nexus, someone would see, and then everyone would decide they knew why I had done it."

Her gaze stays on the place where the lamps bend in different directions.

"Watching is enough today."

exchanges.player: "Thanks for showing me." I watch the wind with her until it is time for dinner. Over the next two days I attend my classes and keep an ordinary routine at Garvey House. On the third evening I join the others for dinner and listen to what has been happening.
exchanges.story:
Ysolde remains at the rail until the dinner bell carries across the quadrangle, following the lamps as they steady and then begin to lean together.

The next two days settle into bells, classrooms, meals, and the repeated creak of Garvey House's stairs. By the third evening, the dining hall has acquired its own habits: Rashid's folio beside his plate, Ashara's practice case against the wall, Aldric arriving with his cuffs still buttoned to the wrist.

Rashid has a folded Academy notice open between the salt cellar and the bread basket.

"I got the instructor's report," he says. "A tether bracket failed. It should have been replaced before the practice group used the court."

Aldric looks down at the notice. "Then the closure was warranted."

"The closure of that court was warranted," Rashid says. "Closing every practice session was not. The director has approved the north ground on Tuesdays and Thursdays, with a supervisor, until the inspection is finished."

Ashara reaches for the bread. "The north ground has no roof."

"Correct. You will not be asked to lend it."

"That is not why I object."

"It is not the only reason."

Rashid's hand rests on the petition tucked beneath the notice.

"The request had thirty-seven signatures by yesterday afternoon. It helped."

Aldric considers that, then nods once. "That is a better outcome than reopening a damaged court."

"Yes," Rashid says. "It is."

exchanges.player: At the next posted Tuesday or Thursday session, after my own classes, I walk out to the north ground to see how the new practice arrangement is working.
exchanges.story:
The north ground sits beyond the public dueling octagon, a broad rectangle of packed earth marked with low rope and white chalk. The afternoon is clear enough for practice, though the wind keeps worrying at the ropes.

Rashid's group has gathered in two uneven lines: Commerce students in rolled sleeves, an Arcana student with her hair tied back, two Conclave students you do not recognize. An Academy supervisor in a padded grey coat watches from the boundary with a whistle at his throat and a written schedule in hand.

"Pairs," Rashid calls. "No full-speed strikes until you can stop on the count."

The first exercise is footwork and distance rather than sparring. At the far end, Dena Arl works through the same marked steps with her splinted wrist held close against her ribs. When a partner drifts inside the chalk line, the supervisor blows the whistle once and sends both of them back to the start without raising his voice.

Rashid moves between the pairs, correcting a shoulder here, a stance there. He is sweating through the collar of his practice shirt by the time the group begins the second drill. The arrangement is slower than a private lesson and louder than the covered court had been, but no one is waiting at the edge for a turn that never comes.

During a water break, Rashid notices you by the rope and lifts two fingers in greeting. Then the supervisor calls the group back into line, and Rashid turns toward a student whose practice blade has slipped loose in his grip.

"Again," Rashid says. "Slower this time."

exchanges.player: I watch until the class finishes. While people are gathering their things, I approach the student with the splinted wrist. "Hi, I'm Rowan. How's the new ground working out for you?"
exchanges.story:
The final whistle sends the pairs apart. Practice blades go back into canvas cases; the supervisor checks off names while the chalk lines blur under scuffing boots.

Dena turns when you approach. Her splint is wrapped in dark leather and brass, leaving the fingers of her injured hand free. She shifts a padded sleeve beneath her other arm.

"Dena," she says. "Hi."

She looks over the north ground, where two students are arguing quietly over whose turn it is to carry the water bucket.

"It's cold, and half of us will track mud into our rooms. But there is a supervisor, and nothing is going to come loose over our heads. I call that an improvement."

Her mouth pulls briefly to one side.

"I want the covered court fixed, not forgotten. Until then, this does."

She tucks the padded sleeve under her uninjured arm and starts toward the path back to the quadrangle.

"If you come to watch again, stand upwind. You can hear the counts better."

exchanges.player: I walk back with her. "I've only seen classes and Garvey House so far. Where do you go when you actually want a good evening?"
exchanges.story:
The path from the north ground joins the quadrangle beneath the low dragon-carved arches. Dena keeps her splinted hand tucked close while she walks, letting the practice crowd flow ahead of her.

"A good evening?" She considers it. "The west gardens, after the lamps come up. There is a tea cart by the wall. The tea is terrible, but the pastry cook sends over whatever won't survive until breakfast."

She glances toward the library, where students are already climbing its front steps with books under their arms.

"People go there when they want to complain about classes without pretending it is study. You can sit by the wall and listen, if that is what you want. Or talk. No one makes you choose in advance."

The corner of her mouth lifts.

"I'm going after I get this dirt out of my boots. You can come along if you want."

exchanges.player: "That sounds good. I'll see you there." I wash up, then go to the tea cart after the lamps come on. I buy a pastry and tea and look for Dena.
exchanges.story:
By the time the garden lamps come on, a small queue has formed at the tea cart. Steam curls from a dented brass kettle, carrying the sharp smell of over-steeped leaves and baked sugar. The vendor passes your tea and paper-wrapped pastry across the counter without slowing the line.

Dena is along the west wall beneath a climbing vine, one shoulder against the stone. Her splint is cleaner now, though it still catches the lamp light at the brass fastenings. Two students nearby are arguing over a Commerce problem neither of them seems eager to solve; Dena listens to them with the expression of someone enjoying the mistakes.

She spots you and lifts her uninjured hand.

"You made it. Good. The best pastries disappear first."

She shifts her satchel from the wall, leaving space beside her. The students at the next stretch of stone continue their argument about shipping costs as the tea cart bell gives a small, impatient ring behind you.

Briar.kind: fresh opening plus 15 adaptive player turns

exchanges.player:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
exchanges.story:
The window in your room has been left open a finger-width. Storm-scent rises from the drop beyond the gardens: rain, cold stone, and the metallic edge of distant lightning. It catches in the lamp-oil air.

The room door stands open a hand's breadth; its swollen lower edge will not quite meet the jamb.

Your primer lies open on the desk beside a stack of clothes sent ahead by people who know your measurements only from letters. A ribbon marks the paragraph on welcome-dinner customs. Lower on the page, the heading *Article Nineteen* waits in severe black type. The Garvey signet at your hand flashes once when the lamp flame shifts, then goes dull again.

Downstairs, a chair leg scrapes across the dining-hall floor. Someone laughs—briefly, then more loudly—and another voice cuts in too low to make out. The house has no trouble sounding occupied without asking permission of its new owner.

Three light knocks sound against the exposed strip of frame.

Seraphel Dawnquill waits in the corridor with one hand resting against the frame. Her white-and-gold sleeve is rolled over the wrist, and the small wings at her back fold neatly enough to clear the wall. Warm light from the stairwell catches in her hair.

“The lamps are lit below,” she says.

Her blue eyes move once over the room, taking in the desk and the open primer without lingering.

“They have begun to argue about seating.
No blood has been spilled.
It is, I think, an encouraging start.”

From the landing comes a clearer burst of conversation. A man's voice says, “There are seventeen places. This cannot be difficult.” Another answers, dry and unmistakably amused, “You have made it difficult by counting them aloud.”

Seraphel's mouth tips at one corner. She steps aside, leaving the door open to the lamp-lit stairs and the noise below.

exchanges.player: "I am Rowan. I would be grateful." I follow Seraphel downstairs and greet the table. "If you need a tie-breaker, I will take whichever seat is nearest the food." I look for an unoccupied place.
exchanges.story:
The dining hall makes seven students look temporarily lost. Seventeen places run down the varnished table beneath candles and working lamps, with bowls of buttered roots, black bread, and a rosemary-dark roast waiting in the middle.

Your greeting turns the argument into a pause.

Rashid vel Amara is standing beside a chair near the roast, one fine-furred hand on its carved back. He looks at the place setting, then at you. “A strategically sound criterion. This one is available.”

Across from it, Ashara vel Kothren leans back in her chair, black-red horns catching the candlelight. Her tail has hooked itself around one of the chair legs. “It is also nearest Rashid. Consider that before committing.”

“I can move,” Rashid says.

“You have spent five minutes refusing to.”

The corner of his mouth pulls despite himself. “I was establishing a principle.”

At the table's far side, a white-haired woman sits so still that the lamplight seems to settle around her. Beside her, an elf with metallic-silver hair has arranged her napkin with surgical care. The smaller fae woman watches the exchange over folded hands, while Aldric Verantus rises from his place in crisp white and gold.

“Rowan Garvey,” he says, with a small formal inclination of his head. “Welcome to Garvey House, and to the Conclave.”

Seraphel takes the chair beside the empty one, tucking her wings close as she sits. “You have been offered the roast,” she says. “This is how friendships begin here.”

Ashara reaches for the bread basket before Rashid can. “That is how arguments begin here.”

The vacant chair waits between Seraphel and Rashid, its plate already warm from the kitchen.

exchanges.player: I take the offered chair and help myself to dinner. I speak to Seraphel beside me. "There is a letter framed in my room. I do not even know who the woman who wrote it was. Is there anyone here who remembers the Garveys as people?"
exchanges.story:
You take the offered chair and pass yourself roast, roots, and a piece of black bread. The meat is peppered hard enough to warm the back of your throat.

Seraphel tears her bread into neat pieces while you speak. For a moment, the only sound from her is the faint brush of feathers as she settles one wing more comfortably against the chair.

“Not I.
I came after the house emptied.
Professor Stone knew some of them.
He is often in the library after supper.”

At the far side of the table, Caelindra lowers her glass. Her violet eyes have been on you since the word Garvey.

“I met a Lady Garvey when I was young,” she says. “She lost a wager to my mother, invented a second wager, and had all her money back before dessert.” One pointed ear lifts slightly. “She did not hurry. That was unusual.”

Rashid glances from Caelindra to the food in front of him. “That sounds like a dangerous family trait.”

“It sounds like bad supervision,” Ashara says, reaching for the salt.

Caelindra ignores them both. Her attention returns to you, more direct now than before.

“Does the letter have a name?”

exchanges.player: "I have not looked closely. I will check afterward." I turn toward Caelindra. "What was the wager?"
exchanges.story:
Caelindra considers the question with the air of someone deciding whether an old annoyance deserves the effort of speech.

“My mother had said that no human poem could make her laugh,” she says at last. “Lady Garvey wagered two gold crowns that she could read one without producing so much as a smile.”

She takes a measured sip of wine.

“The poem was about a bishop, a turnip, and a remarkably unconvincing ghost. My mother laughed once.”

Ashara's hand pauses over the salt cellar. Rashid looks up from his plate.

“Lady Garvey lost the first wager,” Caelindra continues. “Then she immediately wagered the same amount that my mother would ask to hear the poem again before dessert. She did.”

“Efficient,” Rashid says.

“Obnoxious,” Caelindra corrects. “Mother paid. Lady Garvey gave the crowns to a kitchen boy who had been trying not to laugh.”

For the first time, the elf's attention slips from you to the candle flame between you. “I was very young. I thought the poem was idiotic.”

Seraphel folds a torn piece of bread between her fingers. “It sounds as though it had a useful purpose.”

Caelindra's ear turns toward her. “You would say that.”

“I would.”

The servers begin clearing the first empty dishes at the other end of the long table.

exchanges.player: "Wait—if your mother thought no human poem could make her laugh, why would she take the other side of a wager that she would not smile?" I look at Caelindra, curious rather than accusing.
exchanges.story:
Caelindra's fork stops above her plate.

For a beat, she looks at you as though the answer ought to have been obvious. Then a faint color rises beneath the pale gold of her skin.

“You are right,” she says. “I told it badly.”

She sets the fork down with particular care.

“My mother did not say that a human poem could not make her laugh. She said it could not make her show pleasure. Lady Garvey wagered that it could make her smile.”

The elf's gaze shifts to the candle flame.

“The poem produced a laugh at the turnip. It did not produce a smile. Mother declared the wager settled. Lady Garvey declared that a laugh was evidence of a more interesting case.”

“And then she made the second wager,” Seraphel says.

“Yes.” Caelindra reaches for her wine, then pauses. “She wagered that Mother would ask to hear it again before dessert. Mother did so when she thought no one was listening.”

Rashid's brows lift. “Was anyone?”

“Everyone,” Caelindra says. “Lady Garvey had told the entire room what to listen for.”

Ashara lets out a short laugh into her cup.

Caelindra gives her a level look, though the color has not quite left her face. “It was an effective poem. I refuse to defend its literary merit.”

exchanges.player: "That version's funnier. I think I'd have liked her." I finish dinner, then go upstairs and read the framed letter carefully, including its signature. After that I look for Professor Stone in the library.
exchanges.story:
Caelindra's gaze comes back to you.

“Then you may have liked Edda,” she says. “She liked people who noticed the terms of a wager.”

The remark is almost civil. She returns to her dinner before anyone can make more of it.

By the time the last plates have gone, the long table has loosened into smaller conversations and empty chairs. You leave it behind for the quieter second floor.

The letter waits where you saw it, its narrow walnut frame a little crooked above the desk. Up close, the hand is quick and slanted, with several words pressed hard enough to leave dents in the paper.

*Dear great-nephew,*

*If this room ever becomes yours, open the curtains before you decide it is lonely. Garveys have a habit of making houses into mausoleums after a bad year. The people who live here are not yours to arrange, but they may let you share a meal if you ask properly. If the cooks still make the plum tart, take two slices before any diplomat begins explaining why one is sufficient.*

*With unreasonable hope,*

*Edda Garvey*

The ink has faded to brown at the edges, but the signature remains firm.

The library is lit when you reach it. Lamps burn along the lower floor, turning the iron spiral stair into a black corkscrew against shelves and shelves of books. Professor Gareth Stone sits alone at a long table beneath it, a heavy volume open beside a cup gone cold. He has loosened his collar, and his attention is fixed on a page of cramped notes until the sound of your approach draws it up.

His eyes settle briefly on your signet.

“Mr. Garvey,” he says. “I heard we had a new student. What can I help you find?”

exchanges.player: "I'm trying to picture the people whose name I've ended up with. There's a letter from Edda Garvey in my room, and Caelindra says she once won a wager off her mother. Did you know Edda?"
exchanges.story:
Professor Stone's hand stills on the edge of his notes.

“Yes,” he says after a moment. “I knew Edda.”

He closes the heavy book, leaving a ribbon tucked between its pages. The guardedness in his face does not vanish, exactly, but it gives way to something more ordinary.

“She was a better host than most diplomats and a better diplomat than most hosts. She could make people stay at the table after an argument, which is rarer than it sounds.”

His mouth shifts, almost a smile.

“Once, she persuaded a visiting dragon envoy to eat a whole bowl of plum tart by telling him it was an insult to refuse. It was not an insult. She had simply made too much.”

The lamplight trembles across the rim of his cold cup.

“Edda liked wagers because they made everyone declare what they actually believed. She also liked winning them, which was a separate virtue in her view.”

He looks toward the shelves, then back at you. “The version Caelindra told you sounds like her. Edda would have considered getting Lady Vaeyn to ask for a second reading a finer victory than the coins.”

For a few seconds he studies the signet on your hand, not its value but its workmanship.

“Your letter may tell me when she wrote it. May I see it?”

exchanges.player: "It's in a frame. I'll bring it down." I go back to my room, take the framed letter without removing it from the glass, and return to Stone. I set it where he can read it. "You've heard the story about the poem before, then?"
exchanges.story:
Professor Stone draws the lamp nearer, then bends over the frame without touching the glass. His eyes move through the letter once, return to the closing, and stay there.

“No,” he says. “I had not heard that story before tonight.”

He glances up at you.

“I recognized Edda in it. She loved a wager with a second set of terms concealed inside the first. And Lady Vaeyn had a talent for treating a technical distinction as a fortress.”

His attention returns to the slanted hand.

“This is hers. The capitals, especially. She always made a G as though it were trying to occupy more of the page than the other letters allowed.”

The library's upper shelves disappear into the dimness above the lamps. Stone reads the last line again.

“Unreasonable hope,” he says quietly. “She used that phrase when she meant someone ought to try anyway.”

He straightens, resting both hands on the table's edge.

“Edda wrote letters like this to people who had not yet disappointed her. Sometimes to people who did not exist yet.” A small breath leaves him through his nose. “She believed that was a practical habit.”

Beyond the tall windows, a flare of lightning turns the garden paths white for an instant. Stone looks at the framed letter one more time.

“Keep it out of direct sun. The ink will go first at the edges.”

exchanges.player: "I only said she'd won a wager off Caelindra's mother. I hadn't mentioned a poem or a second reading. How did you know that part?"
exchanges.story:
Professor Stone blinks once. Then he takes his hands from the table.

“You are right. You did not.”

He looks briefly toward the library door.

“I came through the common room while dinner was still going. The dining-hall doors were open, and I heard Caelindra tell the story—enough of it, at least. The poem, the laugh, the second wager.”

His jaw tightens, not quite defensively.

“When I said I had not heard it before tonight, I meant exactly that. I should have said that I had heard it tonight.”

He gives the framed letter a little more space on the table, as though correcting its position might improve the explanation.

“I stopped because I heard Edda's name. That does not make the stopping less rude.”

The lamps hiss softly in their glass chimneys.

“I knew Edda. I did not know that particular story until Caelindra told it.”

exchanges.player: "You could've just said that." I leave the frame where he can see it. "Can you tell how old it is, or who she meant it for?"
exchanges.story:
“I could have,” Stone says. “I should have.”

He pulls a brass magnifier from beneath a stack of catalog cards and leans over the frame again. This time he studies the lower margin, where the paper meets the walnut backing.

“There is no date. But the stationery is old Garvey stock; the watermark was discontinued before the collapse. The ink and the frame fit that as well.” He lowers the magnifier. “I could place it within a few years, not a season. Edda was alive when she wrote it.”

His finger hovers above the salutation without touching the glass.

“And I do not think she meant a particular boy. Not by name.”

He sits back in his chair.

“Edda had no great-nephew at the time, at least none anyone expected. She was writing to a possibility: whoever eventually inherited the house and needed someone to say it had once been full of ordinary people.”

Stone glances around the library, at the lamps and high dark shelves.

“That was her habit. She treated an uncertain future as though it were already waiting for tea.”

exchanges.player: "I'd like something concrete I can read. Can you show me a public record with her name in it?"
exchanges.story:
Stone gives a small nod, as if relieved by the simplicity of the request.

“Yes. The public arbitration rolls are on the upper shelves.”

He takes the spiral stair without hurry, one hand grazing the iron rail. A minute later he returns with a broad, red-leather volume dusted pale along its spine. He sets it beside the frame and opens it with the care of someone who has done so many times.

The pages are printed in dense, orderly columns. Stone finds an index, then turns to a marked page.

“Here.”

At the top is a plain heading: *Academy Student Arbitration, Open Session.* Beneath it, a case concerns the withheld wages of a Garvey House laundress after a donor damaged the steam pipes and refused to pay for repairs. The entry names Edda Garvey as the student's advocate for the laundress, and records the decision: wages restored, repairs charged to the donor's household.

Her name appears again at the bottom in dark archival ink. The capital G curls broadly across the line.

“She was in her third year,” Stone says. “That case made the Academy newsletter. The donor's father complained to the Council for a month.”

He shifts the lamp so the page lies fully in its circle of light.

“It is not a grand record. But it is hers.”

exchanges.player: I read the entry, including its date. "May I copy this for my own notes?" If Stone permits it, I copy the entry without removing any pages. Then I thank him, take the framed letter back to my room, put it back, and sleep until morning.
exchanges.story:
The entry is dated *18 Harvest, 391 C.C.* Its language is dry even when the complaint is not: names, charges, testimony, ruling. Edda's name stands at the foot of the page beside the tidy seal of the open session.

“You may copy it,” Stone says. “That is what a public record is for.”

He finds a clean sheet of Academy paper and sets an inkstand within reach of the lamp. He does not turn away while you work, but neither does he hurry you. The scratch of pen on paper joins the quiet tick of cooling glass chimneys.

When the copy is finished, Stone closes the red volume and returns it to the upper shelf himself.

“Keep the date with it,” he says on his way down. “People remember verdicts and lose the years around them.”

He accepts your thanks with a brief nod. By then the library has grown stiller around its pools of lamp light.

You carry the framed letter back through the sleeping house and set it in its crooked place above the desk. The room holds the faint smell of oil and rain. Outside the window, lightning moves inside the storm without finding the ground.

When morning comes, the storm has thinned to a pale bank beyond the gardens. Light lies across the desk, the letter's walnut frame, and the copied page beside it.

exchanges.player: In the morning I wash, dress, and eat breakfast. I attend my first day of classes. Once lessons are finished, I go to the public dueling ground to see what is happening there.
exchanges.story:
Breakfast is quieter than the welcome dinner, with students coming and going around the long table according to separate timetables. The day gathers speed after that.

Professor Windwhisper spends the morning on treaty notices and the difference between an agreement that has been breached and one that has merely become inconvenient. In Practical Rhetoric, Professor Kira makes the room strip flourishes from a public statement until its actual demand is visible. By the final bell, the Academy's corridors have begun to smell of damp wool, chalk, and the wind brought in from the bridges.

The public dueling ground lies open to the afternoon sky: an octagon of packed earth, low rails, and a ranking board nailed beside the gate. Ashara vel Kothren's name holds the top line. Rashid's is several places below it.

Inside the octagon, Ashara practices with a wooden blade against a broad-shouldered Military student. She gives ground once, twice, then catches the next strike on her guard and turns it cleanly aside. The other student retrieves her balance before Ashara moves again.

Near the rail, Rashid stands with a folded sheet of paper and a small cluster of students. Dena Arl is among them, her wrist splinted in pale cloth.

“No names,” Dena says, tapping the paper with her uninjured hand.

“No names,” Rashid answers. “It asks for supervised access. Nothing else.”

She studies his face, then nods and takes the pen he offers.

Beyond them, two students argue quietly over whether the covered court should remain closed at all. A practice blade cracks against another inside the octagon. Ashara's opponent stumbles back a pace, grinning despite herself, and the small crowd at the rail shifts to make room for whoever wants a better view.

exchanges.player: I stay by the rail. I watch the rest of Ashara's practice and listen to Rashid and Dena while they finish with the request. I do not step into their conversation.
exchanges.story:
Ashara's practice does not hurry toward a finish. Her opponent changes tactics twice; Ashara changes with her, less interested in landing a showy strike than in making the other student work for every opening. When the student overreaches, Ashara catches her wrist with the flat of the practice blade and steps back at once.

“Again,” she says.

Near the rail, Dena finishes reading the request.

“Don't put the accident in the second paragraph,” she tells Rashid.

“It isn't in the second paragraph.”

“Or the third.”

Rashid unfolds the page enough to show her. “It says the restriction affects students who use the court outside their track. It asks for supervision. That is all.”

Dena reads it once more, then signs. A Commerce student beside her adds his name after hers; another asks whether the academy will answer by week's end.

“They will answer when they answer,” Rashid says, folding the sheet carefully. “I will file it before the offices close.”

Inside the octagon, Ashara's opponent finally gets a hit against her shoulder. The watching students make a brief, appreciative noise. Ashara gives a single nod, resets her guard, and the practice goes on.

By the time Rashid tucks the request into his coat, Dena has moved toward the shade of the low wall with two friends. Ashara's practice blade knocks sharply against her opponent's, and the ground keeps its separate rhythms: signatures, footwork, and the scrape of boots in packed earth.

exchanges.player: I head back for dinner and let them get on with it. Over the next few days, I attend classes and work on my own writing. At dinner on the fourth evening, I listen for what's happening around the house.
exchanges.story:
The next days acquire a shape. Lessons divide the mornings and afternoons; your own pages gather ink in the spaces between them. Garvey House develops its habits around you: doors opening before dawn, someone practicing scales in an upper room, the late clink of cups carried back from the library.

On the fourth evening, dinner has lost its first-night stiffness. People choose seats without negotiating them. Rain taps lightly at the tall windows.

Rashid has a folded Academy notice beside his plate. Ashara notices it before he has finished his soup.

“They answered?”

“They offered a meeting on Friday.” He taps the notice once. “The athletics office wants the instructor's report and accounts from the students who were there.”

“You have the accounts?”

“Three students will give their own. The request stays about supervised access.”

Across the table, Aldric sets down his spoon. “That seems a reasonable response to an injury.”

Rashid's courtesy settles into place. “It is a response. I would rather it lead somewhere.”

Ashara tears a piece of bread in half. “Do not present it as a verdict before you have the report.”

“I won't.”

“Good.”

At the far end of the table, Seraphel and Caelindra are bent over an open book between their plates. Ysolde has claimed the chair nearest the rain-streaked window and watches the storm move over the gardens. The house carries several conversations at once, none of them waiting for an invitation to continue.

exchanges.player: I leave the request to Rashid. I spend Friday in classes and the library; at dinner that evening, I ask him how the meeting went.
exchanges.story:
Friday passes through lectures, library lamps, and the ordinary work of keeping up. By dinner, rain has cleared from the windows, leaving the garden paths dark and bright-edged beneath the lamps.

When you ask Rashid about the meeting, he has just unfolded his napkin.

“Better than a refusal,” he says. “Not a full reopening.”

He takes a folded notice from his coat and lays it beside his plate.

“The covered court stays closed while Facilities inspect the flooring and equipment. The instructor's report does not assign blame. Starting Monday, students outside the Military track get two supervised sessions a week on the public ground.”

Ashara looks over from her soup. “With whom supervising?”

“A senior Military student and a faculty rotation. The office will review it after two weeks.”

“That is a trial,” she says.

“Yes.” Rashid smooths the notice flat. “It gets people practice time while the actual report is sorted out.”

At the end of the table, Aldric nods once. “That seems measured.”

Rashid's glance flicks toward him. “It is more useful than a closed door.”

Ashara returns to her soup. “Do not mistake a useful beginning for a win.”

“I don't.”

The notice remains between them, its Academy seal catching the candlelight.

Copper.kind: constructed continuity situation followed by three submissions

history.content: At dinner I tell Rashid, with Ashara sitting across from us, "I will be at the press tomorrow at sixth bell. You can find me there then."
Rashid puts a small mark beside the appointment in his notebook. "Sixth bell. I can bring the revised request then." Ashara continues eating; neither of them asks about the printing.
Later I go alone to speak to the press steward.

The pressroom is empty except for the steward, Sela. She shows you a crack in the platen. "I cannot run this safely tomorrow. We will have to use the hand press in the west workshop. It is free at fourth bell, if that suits you." The door is shut; the workshop passage outside is quiet.

"Fourth bell in the west workshop is fine. Please leave the change to me; I will tell Rashid myself." I return to my room and keep the change to myself. The next morning I bring three manuscript pages to the library to show Caelindra. My unfinished story concerns a lighthouse keeper who leaves his post to obtain medicine for a sick neighbor. His replacement fails to arrive, and the lighthouse remains dark until midnight. I have not written what happens to any ships or how the story ends.

Caelindra sits at the library window with a book propped against the inkwell. She lays it face-down when you set the pages on the table. "I have a quarter of an hour." She turns the first page. Rashid is elsewhere at morning practice, and nobody else is within earshot.

fixture.provenance: Pilot-authored held-out state for manuscript ownership, silent thoughts, and a privately changed appointment. Not counted among fresh long sessions.

exchanges.player: "I am not looking for a verdict on whether he is a good person. Does the situation hold your interest so far?" I let Caelindra read the three pages. Privately, I wonder whether I have made the keeper too obviously resemble Rashid; I do not say that aloud.
exchanges.story:
Caelindra finishes the third page, then turns back to the first and reads its last paragraph again. Her own book remains face-down beside the inkwell. The window draft lifts a corner of your manuscript; she pins it beneath two pale fingers.

"Yes," she says at last. "The keeper's reason is ordinary enough that I believe he would leave. That is more interesting than making him a fool."

She lays the pages into a neat stack but keeps her hand on them. "There are already three claims on him: the neighbor, the light, and the person expected to relieve him. You haven't told me which claim he thinks he has failed. I want to know whether he understands that before midnight."

A cart rattles beyond the library shelves. Caelindra glances toward the iron stair, as if measuring the passing minutes, then looks back at the manuscript.

"I also want to know why the replacement does not come. Have you decided that?"

exchanges.player: "Thank you. I will think about the replacement." I take the manuscript back and leave her to her book. At lunch I find Rashid. "Are we still set for this afternoon?" I have not told anyone besides Sela about the changed time or location.
exchanges.story:
Rashid occupies one end of the dining table, his lunch cooling beside an open notebook. Names run down one page in a small, precise hand, with tick marks crowded into the margin. He looks up as you approach.

"Sixth bell at the press," he says. "I've got the revised request."

He pulls a folded sheet from the notebook and smooths it against the table. The first paragraph asks for supervised access for students outside the Military track; below it, the request promises a roster, an instructor, and an equipment inspection before each session.

"I left out the injury," he says. "We don't have the report, and I won't make a case from rumors. If they want to defend the restriction, they can tell us what failed."

He refolds the page with the same care he used to open it. "Ashara can keep her booking. This isn't about taking it from her." A serving dish passes between two students farther down the table. Rashid closes the notebook and slides it beneath his tray.

"Sixth bell," he repeats.

exchanges.player: "The press has a cracked platen. Sela moved my own work to fourth bell in the west workshop. I can read your revised request now, but I will not print it; my booking is for the story. You will need to arrange the request separately." I hold out my hand for the sheet.
exchanges.story:
Rashid's fingers stay on the sheet after you hold out your hand. The dining hall's noon clatter fills the pause: knives against plates, a chair scraping stone. Then he lets the paper go.

"I wasn't asking you to give up your booking," he says. His voice is even. "I thought we would read the wording at sixth, and I would arrange the printing afterward."

He shuts the notebook, then opens it again to copy the west workshop's location beneath an existing note. "Fourth bell. Fine. I'll ask Sela whether the hand press has another opening, or take it to Commerce. I need it printed, not treated as a favor."

Fresh ink darkens the request's headings; its margins carry small, crowded revisions and a blank space beside the signatures.

Rashid taps the folded pages now in your hand. "Read it. I kept it to supervised access and left the injury out. If you see a weakness, tell me before I put my name under it."

Only then does he pick up his fork again.
